lesson.title: Spleen, hilum and splenic ligaments
lesson.summary: The spleen develops in dorsal mesogastric mesenchyme, not as an endodermal gut-tube outgrowth.

steps.title: Spleen
steps.body: The spleen is an intraperitoneal lymphoid organ in the left hypochondrium, commonly related to ribs 9-11. It has diaphragmatic and visceral surfaces, a hilum, and peritoneal ligaments to stomach and posterior abdominal wall.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Visceral surface relates to stomach, left kidney, colon, and pancreatic tail. Gastrosplenic ligament carries short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels. Splenorenal ligament carries splenic vessels and pancreatic tail. Splenic artery is a tortuous branch of the celiac trunk. Branches of the splenic artery: pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, left gastro-omental artery, and terminal splenic branches entering the splenic hilum.

steps.title: Why is the spleen's relation to the lower ribs important without making it an intrathoracic organ?
steps.body: The spleen lies below the diaphragm but projects deep to the left lower ribs, classically around ribs 9-11 with its long axis near the tenth rib. The diaphragm separates it from pleura and lung above. A surface view can therefore place ribs over an abdominal organ without relocating that organ into the thorax. Its thin capsule, vascular parenchyma and nearby pancreatic tail explain the importance of regional relationships. Spleen size and position vary with body form and disease.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: The spleen develops in dorsal mesogastric mesenchyme, not as an endodermal gut-tube outgrowth. Its adult celiac supply does not make it a foregut epithelial derivative. The gastrosplenic ligament connects it with the stomach and carries short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels. The splenorenal ligament contains splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail. Naming the ligament predicts the adjacent structures that must be considered in regional anatomy.
